candidates.title: rollup CLI keeps the outputs Merkle tree in an undocumented /tmp/merkle.dat, updates it after the output yield and silently ignores load/save failures, so a lost or short file resets the tree and the next accept writes a wrong outputs Merkle root
candidates.component: machine-guest-tools v0.18.1-test1: sys-utils/rollup/rollup.cpp (rollup command-line tool) with libcmt merkle/util
candidates.location: sys-utils/rollup/rollup.cpp class rollup: constructor calls cmt_rollup_load_merkle(&m_rollup, "/tmp/merkle.dat") and ignores its return value; destructor calls cmt_rollup_save_merkle(...) and ignores its return value. libcmt/src/merkle.c cmt_merkle_load reads straight into *me via cmt_util_read_whole_file and only afterwards checks length != sizeof *me (partial overwrite on a short file). libcmt/src/util.c cmt_util_write_whole_file opens with fopen("wb") (truncate first, write later, not atomic).
candidates.description: Each `rollup` invocation is a separate process. The outputs tree (leaf count plus 63 subtree hashes, 2024 bytes) is the only state that links outputs emitted by different invocations, and it lives in /tmp/merkle.dat, which neither the tool's help nor the manual mentions. (1) If the file cannot be read (missing, unreadable, shorter than 2024 bytes), cmt_rollup_load_merkle fails and the CLI continues with the empty tree (or a tree partially overwritten by the short read). The next `rollup notice/voucher` returns index 0 again, and the next `rollup accept` writes to the tx buffer a root that omits every output accepted before. (2) The tree is saved only in the destructor, after the automatic yield that already emitted the output to the host, and the save truncates the file before writing; a failed write (ENOSPC/ENOMEM on tmpfs under memory pressure, EACCES when the tool runs as another user) or a kill between the yield and the save (OOM killer, SIGPIPE while printing the index to a closed pipe) leaves the host with an emitted output that the guest tree does not contain, or with an empty file. In all cases the tool reports success (exit 0, index printed) and the application has no way to notice.
candidates.trigger: The application's own guest environment, driven by inputs: an application that, as documented, uses the rollup CLI and treats /tmp as scratch space (e.g. removes its temporary files with rm -rf /tmp/* after each input, or lets input-driven data use tmpfs/RAM until a write fails), or whose `rollup notice` process is killed or gets SIGPIPE after the yield. No emulator or host action is involved.
candidates.reachability: Reachable from a valid template whose guest uses the rollup CLI (the manual's calculator and the harness valid-template app.sh do). Demonstrated on the host with libcmt's mock driver: two `rollup notice` calls return indices 0 and 1; after deleting the tree file the third returns index 0, i.e. the tree was silently reset. Whether an input can cause the file loss depends on the application (cleanup of /tmp, memory exhaustion, process kill); no input can do it for an application that never touches /tmp and stays far from memory limits.
candidates.rating_steps: 1 Out of scope? The exclusion 'An application that is not correctly designed, other than through a defect in guest software that section 3 puts in scope' does not apply if the application is correctly designed against the tool's documentation, which never says that /tmp/merkle.dat must be preserved or that a failed save is silent. 2 Role: AUDIT.md table: 'machine-guest-tools v0.18.1-test1 | Guest software'. Section 3: 'A defect in them is in scope only where an application depends on them as documented, and would be correctly designed if they worked as documented. A defect that lets an input make such an application deviate from the rollup interface is Critical, as an R7 deviation in the rx buffer, the tx buffer and the yield interface. Any other defect in them is Low.' 3 High/Medium cases: none apply to guest software. 4 Critical: the deviation is from 'When it accepts, it leaves in the tx buffer the outputs Merkle root of every output it accepted. That includes the outputs its template already commits to, and the outputs emitted while processing the inputs it accepted' (definition of correctly designed application) and R7 'The rx buffer, the tx buffer, and the yield interface (contents, lengths, and reason encoding)'. It is Critical if triage accepts that an input can trigger the loss for an application that uses the CLI as documented (an application that clears its /tmp scratch files, or an input that drives guest memory to exhaustion so that the save fails). 5 Low otherwise ('a defect in guest software that only an application outside its intended use can reach'). Two readings: Critical if clearing /tmp or reaching tmpfs/RAM limits counts as documented use; Low if the implicit /tmp/merkle.dat dependency is considered part of the intended use. Deciding fact: whether the CLI's documentation (help text embedded in doc/README.md) is read as permitting the application to manage /tmp.
candidates.claimed_severity: Low (Critical under the reading that an application clearing /tmp, or an input that exhausts guest memory, is within documented use)
candidates.threat_to_goal: The goal protects 'accept an output that the settled state does not commit to' and A5 'the referee accepts every output that the settled state commits to'. With a reset tree the settled state commits to a root that omits outputs the application accepted earlier, so those vouchers and notices can never be executed or validated on-chain, and new outputs reuse their indices; the honest operator settles that state correctly (the emulator is not at fault), so the loss is entirely in what the application gets.
candidates.evidence: Built the CLI on the host from the tag with libcmt's io-mock driver and the tree path redirected to the scratch directory (exp/rollup-p). `echo '{"payload":"0x01"}' | rollup notice` twice -> {"index":0}, {"index":1}; rm merkle.dat; third call -> {"index":0}. A 100-byte truncated file is loaded partially without any error. Source review shows both return codes ignored and the save happening after the yield.
candidates.test_idea: Inside a machine built from the guest-tools rootfs: entrypoint `rollup accept; echo '{"payload":"0x01"}' | rollup notice; rollup accept; rm -f /tmp/*; echo '{"payload":"0x02"}' | rollup notice; rollup accept` (or equivalently make the file unreadable). Deliver two advance inputs, collect outputs with the cartesi-machine CLI, and assert that the tx-buffer root at the second accept equals the root of the two emitted output hashes (the hash-tree frontier of both leaves) and that the second notice index is 1. On v0.18.1-test1 the root equals that of a single leaf and the index is 0, so the test exits 1; a fixed tool must either keep the tree or fail loudly (non-zero exit before the yield) so the application can reject.

candidates.title: rollup CLI --utf8-payload: an input whose payload is not valid UTF-8 makes `rollup accept/reject/finish` consume the input and then exit 1 with no request printed
candidates.component: machine-guest-tools v0.18.1-test1: sys-utils/rollup/rollup.cpp (write_advance_state / encode_payload with nlohmann json dump)
candidates.location: sys-utils/rollup/rollup.cpp: encode_payload returns the raw bytes for encoding::utf8; write_advance_state builds a json and calls j.dump(2), which with nlohmann 3.12's default error_handler_t::strict throws type_error.316 on invalid UTF-8; the exception is caught in finish_request_and_get_next after cmt_rollup_finish has already yielded and received the input.
candidates.description: In --utf8-payload mode the tool cannot represent a payload that is not valid UTF-8. It discovers this only after the manual rx-accepted yield has returned with the new input, so the input is delivered and gone, but the tool prints an exception message to stderr, writes nothing to stdout and exits 1. A failure of the yield itself and a failure to encode the payload are indistinguishable to the caller. An application that loops on `rollup --utf8-payload accept` and ignores or retries on a failure accepts the input without ever seeing it; one that runs under `set -e` exits, the init script powers the machine off, and the application halts for every later input. Any input sender can choose such a payload (InputBox payloads are arbitrary bytes).
candidates.trigger: Any input sender: an advance input whose payload contains a byte sequence that is not valid UTF-8 (e.g. 0xff), sent to an application that uses `rollup --utf8-payload` as the manual's calculator does.
candidates.reachability: Reachable from any valid template that uses the CLI in --utf8-payload mode; payload bytes are unrestricted. The manual's own calculator (doc/recipes calc.sh) survives it because it treats an empty request as an error and rejects, so the damage depends on how the application handles the tool's failure.
candidates.rating_steps: 1 Out of scope? The stall exclusion ('The stall of an application that halts ... and what the application loses by it') covers applications that halt by themselves; here guest software causes the halt or the unprocessed accept, which section 3 brings back into scope only for applications that use the tool as documented. 2 Role: 'machine-guest-tools v0.18.1-test1 | Guest software'. 3 High/Medium: none for guest software. 4 Critical if an application using --utf8-payload as documented ('encode/decode <data> fields in JSON values as UTF-8 text') is considered correctly designed for arbitrary inputs: the input then makes it deviate from 'After each input, it yields manually with the accepted or the rejected reason' (halt) or decode the input wrongly (an accepted input that the application never saw), R7 'the rx buffer ... and the yield interface'. 5 Low if the documented scope of --utf8-payload is text payloads only, since the manual's encoding section says to use hex or base64 'when payloads contain arbitrary binary data rather than text'; an application that cannot trust its inputs to be text would then be outside the intended use. Deciding fact: whether the tool is documented as usable for untrusted payloads in utf8 mode.
candidates.claimed_severity: Low (Critical under the reading that --utf8-payload is documented for arbitrary inputs)
candidates.threat_to_goal: Does not affect the emulator or the honest operator. It threatens what the application gets: an input sender can make an application built on the documented utf8 mode halt permanently or skip its own processing of an input it nevertheless accepts.
candidates.evidence: Host build of the CLI from the tag with libcmt io-mock: `CMT_INPUTS=0:good.bin rollup --utf8-payload accept` prints the request (payload "hello", rc 0); with payload 68ff6c6c6f it prints `[json.exception.type_error.316] invalid UTF-8 byte at index 1: 0xFF` and exits 1 after the mock delivered the input; the default hex mode prints "0x68ff6c6c6f".
candidates.test_idea: Machine with entrypoint `while :; do rollup --utf8-payload accept > /tmp/req || { echo FAIL > /dev/console; exit 3; }; jq -Rs '{payload:.}' /tmp/req | rollup notice >/dev/null; done`; deliver an advance input with payload 0xff; assert the machine reaches a manual rx-accepted yield (or a defined rejection) rather than halting, i.e. the tool must either encode the payload losslessly (e.g. replacement or escaping documented) or fail before accepting the input. Fails (halt) on v0.18.1-test1.

candidates.title: rollup CLI voucher accepts a "value" shorter than 32 bytes, places it in the most significant bytes and fills the rest of the uint256 with uninitialized stack memory
candidates.location: sys-utils/rollup/rollup.cpp decode_hex32 (`if (s.size() > 2 + 64) throw`, accepts any shorter even-length 0x string) and write_voucher (`cmt_abi_u256_t value;` uninitialized, then `memcpy(value.data, value_bytes.data(), value_bytes.size())`).
candidates.description: decode_hex32 only bounds the maximum length, so "0x05" or even "0x" are accepted. write_voucher copies the decoded bytes to the start of an uninitialized big-endian cmt_abi_u256_t and passes it to cmt_rollup_emit_voucher, so the encoded Voucher value is 0x05 followed by 31 bytes of stack garbage (pointers and fragments of the JSON input in the host build). rollup-http-server, given the same "0x05", right-aligns it and encodes 5. The voucher's value (wei the application contract sends when the voucher executes) is therefore wrong and depends on uninitialized memory; it is deterministic inside the machine (no R1 issue) but not what the application asked for.
candidates.trigger: An application that passes a minimally formatted value (e.g. computed from an input amount with printf '0x%x') to `rollup voucher`; the help and manual say <hex-uint256> is 'a big-endian 32-byte unsigned integer in hex', so a short value is outside the documented format although the tool accepts it without error.
candidates.reachability: Requires the application to pass a short value. The amount itself can come from an input, but only an application that departs from the documented 32-byte format reaches the defect.
candidates.rating_steps: 1 Out of scope? No exclusion applies to the tool's own defect. 2 Role: 'machine-guest-tools v0.18.1-test1 | Guest software'. 3 High/Medium: none for guest software. 4 Critical only if a short value counts as documented use ('A defect that lets an input make such an application deviate from the rollup interface is Critical, as an R7 deviation in ... the tx buffer'): the output bytes in the tx buffer would not be the voucher the application requested. 5 Low: the documented format is 32 bytes, so this is 'a defect in guest software that only an application outside its intended use can reach'; the missing validation and the use of uninitialized memory are still real defects.
candidates.threat_to_goal: No threat to the emulator or the honest operator; a voucher can transfer an arbitrary garbage amount of the application's funds when an application formats values the way rollup-http-server accepts.
candidates.evidence: Host build with io-mock: `{"destination":"0x11..11","value":"0x05","payload":"0x"}` | rollup voucher -> encoded value word 05d5e0934c5600005b000000...78000000...6174696f6e223a00 ("ation\":" from the JSON input); value "0x" -> 20a576035c550000...; a full 32-byte value encodes correctly.
candidates.test_idea: Run `echo '{"destination":"0x1111111111111111111111111111111111111111","value":"0x05","payload":"0x"}' | rollup voucher` in the machine and assert that either the tool exits non-zero before yielding, or the emitted output's value word equals uint256(5). On v0.18.1-test1 the output exists with a different value word.

candidates.title: libcmt cmt_gio_request and `rollup gio` accept any domain, including the rollup manual reasons 1 (rx-accepted), 2 (rx-rejected) and 4 (exception); the CLI also truncates the JSON domain to uint16 (65537 -> 1)
candidates.component: machine-guest-tools v0.18.1-test1: libcmt/src/rollup.c cmt_gio_request; sys-utils/rollup/rollup.cpp gio()
candidates.location: libcmt/src/rollup.c cmt_gio_request: `.cmd = HTIF_YIELD_CMD_MANUAL, .reason = req->domain, .data = req->id_length` with the id copied to the start of tx, no check of domain; rollup.cpp gio(): `ji["domain"].get<uint16_t>()` (nlohmann static_cast, 65537 and -65535 both become 1). rollup-http-server validates domain >= 0x10, libcmt and the CLI do not.
candidates.description: A GIO request with domain 1 is a manual yield with the rx-accepted reason whose tx buffer holds the GIO id instead of the outputs Merkle root, and whose data length is the id length; domain 2 rejects the current input, domain 4 is an exception. In PRT the rx-accepted yield is the fixed point from which A5 extracts the outputs Merkle root, so the id bytes would be settled as the root, and libcmt's own cached root (finish_outputs_merkle_root) no longer matches the tx buffer. The CLI's silent uint16 truncation turns out-of-range domains into these reserved reasons.
candidates.trigger: An application that issues GIO requests with a domain it does not control precisely (e.g. derived from an input, or an out-of-range JSON number passed to `rollup gio`).
candidates.reachability: Needs an application that uses GIO with a reserved or out-of-range domain; the CLI help documents domain only as <number>. GIO responses are not part of the PRT verified history, so a GIO-using application already stalls in PRT; only the reserved-reason aliasing changes the settled state.
candidates.rating_steps: 1 Out of scope? 'The stall of an application that halts, yields manually with a reason other than accepted or rejected, or never yields' covers ordinary GIO domains, not domains 1/2. 2 Role: 'machine-guest-tools v0.18.1-test1 | Guest software'. 3 High/Medium: none. 4 Critical only if an input can choose the domain in an application using GIO as documented; then the yield reason and tx contents deviate from the rollup interface (R7 'the tx buffer, and the yield interface (contents, lengths, and reason encoding)'). 5 Low otherwise: requires an application outside the intended use of GIO.
candidates.threat_to_goal: A wrongly encoded yield reason could make a state settle with guest data in place of the outputs Merkle root (A5), making the application's outputs unprovable; no effect on the emulator or the honest operator.
candidates.evidence: Source review; nlohmann 3.12 bundled with the tag converts 65537, -65535 and 1.9 to uint16 1 (host test exp/j.cpp). libcmt passes the domain straight into the HTIF reason field.
candidates.test_idea: Entrypoint `rollup accept; echo '{"domain":65537,"id":"0xaabb"}' | rollup gio`; deliver one input; assert the machine is not at a manual yield with reason rx-accepted whose tx word differs from the outputs Merkle root (expected: the tool rejects reserved/out-of-range domains). Fails on v0.18.1-test1.

candidates.title: rollup-http-client send_notice/send_voucher/send_delegate_call_voucher/send_report return () and ignore HTTP error statuses, so an application cannot detect that an output was not emitted and accepts the input anyway
candidates.location: rollup-http-client/src/client.rs send_voucher, send_delegate_call_voucher, send_notice, send_report: on Ok(res) they only parse the body as IndexResponse into a debug log (no status check, no return value); rollup-http-server/src/http_service.rs returns 400 when libcmt fails (e.g. -ENOBUFS when the encoded output exceeds the 2 MiB tx buffer, or the 5 MiB JSON limit).
candidates.description: When rollup-http-server cannot emit an output (encoded output larger than the tx buffer, invalid hex, JSON body over the limit), it answers 400 and no output yield happens. The client functions swallow this: their signature returns nothing and the failure only appears as a failed deserialization in a debug log. An application using the client as documented then sends /finish accept, committing an outputs Merkle root without the output it believes it emitted, and with every later output index shifted relative to the application's expectations.
candidates.trigger: An input whose processing produces an output that the server refuses, typically an output whose size grows with the input or with accumulated state, in an application that uses rollup-http-client.
candidates.reachability: InputBox inputs are at most 64 KiB, so a direct echo cannot exceed the 2 MiB tx buffer; the application must amplify input into a larger output. The rollup-http-client crate is a library apps may depend on; the echo-dapp example uses it.
candidates.rating_steps: 1 Out of scope? 'An application that tries to exhaust the honest operator through the number of its outputs' does not apply; this is about a lost output. 2 Role: 'machine-guest-tools v0.18.1-test1 | Guest software'. 3 High/Medium: none. 4 Critical only if an application that uses the client as documented and stays within the documented output size can be made to lose an output by an input; the oversize case is arguably the application exceeding a limit. 5 Low otherwise: the server and libcmt behave correctly (no yield, error reported); the defect is the client's error swallowing.
candidates.threat_to_goal: No threat to the emulator or the honest operator; an application can accept an input whose voucher it believes was emitted, losing funds-moving outputs silently.
candidates.evidence: Source review only (no Rust toolchain build performed).
candidates.test_idea: Unit test against a mock server returning 400 for /notice: assert send_notice surfaces an error (Result::Err). On v0.18.1-test1 it returns () with no indication.

not_covered: The guest kernel's /dev/cmio driver (cartesi/linux) that libcmt's ioctls rely on: out of scope (Linux kernel); the libcmt pack/unpack of the HTIF fields was checked against the emulator's send_cmio_response layout (reason<<32 | length) only.

Nothing was run inside a Cartesi Machine: all experiments used host builds of libcmt with io-mock; the riscv64 binaries in work/images/rootfs.ext2 and the .deb/.tar.gz were not compared with the tag source.

rollup-http-server and rollup-http-client were reviewed by reading only (no Rust build/run); actix-web behaviour on handler panics (e.g. &payload[2..] on a payload shorter than 2 bytes) and concurrency of overlapping /notice and /finish requests were not exercised.
Rust dependency versions (actix-web, validator, hex, hyper) were not audited.

echo-dapp (example), ioctl-echo-loop (test tool), and the misc tools (hex, memoryrange/flashdrive/nvram, readmmap, writemmap, readbe64/writebe64, xhalt) were skimmed or not read; they do not implement the rollup interface for applications.
libcmt keccak.c was validated only indirectly (function selectors and the 65-entry pristine hash table recomputed and matched); no differential fuzzing against another keccak.

libcmt ABI encoders/decoders were reviewed by reading and one host encoding check of a Voucher; no fuzzing of cmt_abi_* decoders with arbitrary rx contents (inputs are canonical InputBox encodings, but non-canonical offsets are accepted without error).

The base64/hex codecs throw inside std::string::resize_and_overwrite, which the standard makes undefined behaviour; libstdc++'s implementation tolerates it, so it was not reported; the guest toolchain's libstdc++ version was not checked.
libcmt's Lua/FFI bindings (tools/prepare-ffi.sh, ffi.h) and pkg-config files were not reviewed.
Inspect-state handling in the tools was not examined beyond confirming it is outside PRT history.
